texto: I'd been driving for almost 11 hours when the
detour signs pushed me off the interstate.
The road narrowed to two lanes, then the radio
lost its station, and for a long time the
only light out there was my own headlights.
Around two in the morning, I saw a gas station sign glowing over the fields.
The pumps were on, the store was dark, and there was one other car parked by the air
machine with its engine running and nobody inside.
This was in October, about six years ago.
I was 24 and moving back home to Missouri after a job in Colorado fell apart.
Everything I owned was in the backseat of a Corolla with a cracked windshield.
I'd planned to stop for the night in a motel somewhere
in western Kansas, but I kept telling
myself one more hour, and by the time the detour
came up, I was too tired to be smart
about it.
I pulled up to the pump, farthest from the other car.
It was an older station wagon, dark green with wood panels on the sides and a bumper
sticker that said, Proud Parent of an Honor Student,
with the name of the school scratched
off.
The exhaust was rising in the cold.
The headlights were off, but the dome light was
on, and I could see a jacket on the passenger
seat and a fast food bag on the dashboard.
I figured whoever it belonged to was in the
bathroom around the side of the building.
I filled the tank and waited.
I don't know why I waited.
I think I wanted to see someone walk back to that car, just so I could stop thinking
about it.
Nobody came.
The pump clicked off, the screen asked if I
wanted a receipt, and the whole time that
engine kept idling, steady, like it had been running for hours.
I didn't go check the bathroom.
I got back in my car and left.
About twenty minutes later, the detour signs ended at a truck stop.
It was the first real building I'd seen in a long time.
A diner on one side, a couple of semis parked
out back with their running lights on, and
a sign that said, Open 24 hours, with two of the letters burned out.
I parked near the entrance because I needed
coffee, and I needed to sit somewhere with
people for a while.
Inside, it was warm and smelled like burnt coffee and bacon grease.
There was a trucker at the counter, reading
his phone, an older man asleep in a booth
by the window, and one waitress.
Her name tag said D. She looked about fifty,
and she called me Honey before I'd even sat
down.
I took a booth facing the door, ordered coffee
and a slice of pie, and started looking at
the map on my phone, trying to figure out how far I was from anything.
That's when the couple came in.
They were young, maybe my age.
The guy wore a gray hoodie, and the girl had
on a denim jacket that was too thin for the
weather.
It had started to rain outside, and the shoulders
of their jackets were dark with it.
They were arguing in that low, tight way people argue in public.
As they walked past my booth, the girl said,
Every single time, Ray.
Every single time.
He didn't answer.
They sat two booths down from me, across the
aisle, and D. went over with menus and two
waters like it was nothing.
I didn't think much about it.
I ate my pie.
I heard bits of their conversation, something about
a wrong turn and whose idea it had been
to leave so late.
The girl had a laugh that wasn't really a laugh.
At one point, Ray said, We'll be fine.
We're almost there.
She didn't say anything back.
After a while, I got up to use the restroom.
It was at the end of a short hallway past the kitchen.
I remember the hallway because one of the fluorescent
lights was flickering, and there
was a corkboard on the wall with business cards and a flyer for a missing dog.
I was in there maybe three or four minutes.
I washed my hands, splashed water on my face,
and looked at myself in the mirror, thinking
I really needed to find a bed.
When I came out and walked back toward my booth, the bell over the front door rang.
It was them, the same couple, gray hoodie, thin
denim jacket, the shoulders of both jackets
dark with rain.
They walked in the same way, him a step ahead,
her a little behind with her arms crossed,
and as they passed me, the girl said, Every single time, Ray, every single time.
I stopped in the aisle.
I looked over at the booth two down from mine, where they'd been sitting.
It was empty.
No menus, no glasses, no wet rings on the table.
It had been wiped down like nobody had used it all night.
They sat in that same booth.
Dee came over with two menus and two waters, and
she smiled at them, and she said, Evening
you two.
Rough night out there?
Exactly how you'd greet someone who just walked in.
I sat down because I didn't know what else to do.
My coffee was still there.
My plate was still there.
I watched them.
I kept waiting for one of them to look at me,
or laugh, or for this to turn into some
kind of joke.
Ray was rubbing his eyes.
The girl was looking out the window at the parking lot.
They were having the same conversation.
Wrong turn.
Leaving too late.
And then Ray said, We'll be fine.
We're almost there.
I looked at the trucker at the counter.
He hadn't looked up from his phone the whole time.
The old man in the window booth was still asleep.
Nobody else in that room seemed to think anything was wrong.
I left a twenty on the table and walked out.
I didn't wait for change.
When I got outside, the rain had stopped, and the parking lot was dry.
Completely dry.
No puddles.
Nothing wet on my windshield.
I stood there for a second, looking at the ground.
Then I got in my car, locked the doors, and sat
with the engine running for a long time.
I didn't want to drive past that gas station again.
I didn't want to go back inside, either.
So I just sat there until the sky started to
turn gray, and then I followed the signs
back to the interstate.
I didn't pass the gas station on the way back.
I took the same road.
I'm sure of that.
It just wasn't there.
I had a dash cam back then, one of those cheap ones
that records over itself every few hours.
When I finally got home and checked it, most
of that night had already been overwritten.
The only file left starts as I pull into the truck
stop parking lot at 2.14 in the morning.
I park, the camera keeps recording, and about
a minute later, the dark green station wagon
pulls into the spot right in front of me.
Engine running, dome light on, nobody inside.
The date on that clip is October 14th.
The year is the one before I ever drove that road.
I still drive that interstate a couple of times a year.
If the detour signs are up, I don't take them.
I find the last town before the exit, I park
somewhere well lit, and I sleep in my car
until morning.
